questions.stem: Why do young people need special protection under the law?
options: They are still developing physically and mentally and are more vulnerable to exploitation and harm
They are not covered by the criminal law until they turn 18, so other laws must protect them
They have no legal rights of their own, so the law treats them as the legal property of their parents
They are more likely than adults to be wealthy, so they need protection from losing their money
questions.explanation: Young people's immaturity and dependence make them vulnerable to abuse, neglect and exploitation, so laws protect them in areas such as care, work and contracts. Children aged 10 and over can be criminally responsible, and children have rights of their own.

questions.stem: Under the Minors (Property and Contracts) Act 1970 (NSW), a contract made by a person under 18 is generally binding on them if:
options: their parents were told about it afterwards
it was made in writing and signed by them
it was for an amount of less than $1,000
it was for their benefit when it was made
questions.explanation: A contract that benefits the minor when made, such as one for necessary goods or services, is presumptively binding. This protects young people from being held to unfair bargains while still allowing them to make useful contracts.

questions.stem: Under section 49 of the Minors (Property and Contracts) Act 1970 (NSW), a doctor who treats a 14-year-old with the young person's own consent:
options: can rely on that consent as a defence if later sued for treating without parental consent
commits a criminal offence, because no one under 16 may consent to any form of medical treatment
must obtain an order of the Children's Court before any treatment can lawfully begin
may treat the young person only if the treatment is free and paid for by Medicare
questions.explanation: The Act treats the consent of a young person aged 14 or over as effective protection for the practitioner, reflecting evolving capacity. For younger children, the common law test of whether the child understands the treatment applies.

questions.stem: Under the Education Act 1990 (NSW), a young person who has completed Year 10 must, until they turn 17:
options: stay enrolled at school full-time in Year 11 and Year 12, whatever their other plans are
obtain the permission of the Children's Court if they want to leave school early to work
stay at home with their parents, who are then legally responsible for providing their education
stay at school, be in approved education or training, or be in paid work, or a mix of these
questions.explanation: The school leaving rules require young people to complete Year 10 and then remain in school, training or employment, or a combination, until 17. The rules aim to protect young people's future opportunities.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the concept of evolving capacity?
options: Young people have the same legal capacity as adults from birth, so the law makes no distinction of any kind based on age
Young people's capacity decreases as they get older, so the law gives more rights to younger children
A young person's capacity is fixed by a court at age 10 and cannot change until the person turns 18
As young people mature, they become able to make more decisions for themselves, and the law gives them more rights
questions.explanation: Article 5 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child refers to the evolving capacities of the child. NSW law reflects this with different ages for consent to treatment, leaving school, driving and voting.

questions.stem: In NSW, at what age can a young person apply for a learner driver licence?
questions.explanation: A young person can get a learner licence at 16 and progress through provisional licences before a full licence. Graduated licensing reflects evolving capacity and road safety concerns.

questions.stem: Which is a common reason young people come into contact with the legal system as offenders?
options: Factors such as disadvantage, unstable housing and disengagement from school increase the risk of offending
Young people are charged with more serious violent offences than adults, which makes them the main offender group
Young people are legally required to report to police every month, which brings them into frequent contact
Young people cannot be victims of crime under NSW law, so all their contact with police is as offenders
questions.explanation: Offending by young people is linked to risk factors such as poverty, family violence, homelessness, substance use and leaving school early. Young people also have contact with the law as victims, witnesses and in care matters.

questions.stem: In NSW, the age of criminal responsibility is:
options: 14 years
16 years
10 years
12 years
questions.explanation: Under section 5 of the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW), a child under 10 cannot be guilty of an offence. Children aged 10 to 13 are also protected by the presumption of doli incapax.

questions.stem: Under the presumption of doli incapax, a child aged 10 to 13 is presumed incapable of committing a crime unless:
options: the child is found to have committed the same act more than once before
the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt the child knew the act was seriously wrong
the child admits to police that they committed the act during a recorded police interview
the child's parents fail to attend court on the day the charge is first heard
questions.explanation: The prosecution must rebut the presumption with evidence that the child knew the conduct was seriously wrong, not merely naughty. The High Court confirmed this in RP v The Queen (2016).

questions.stem: Which argument is most often made for raising the age of criminal responsibility above 10?
options: Young children lack maturity, and early contact with the system increases the likelihood of reoffending
Children under 14 never commit any offences, so laws about them are no longer needed
Raising the age would allow children to be sent to adult prisons, which would improve deterrence
International law requires every child under 18 to be released if they commit any offence
questions.explanation: Advocates point to brain development research and evidence that detaining young children entrenches offending, and the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child recommends a minimum age of at least 14. Opponents argue the community needs protection from serious offending by some children.

questions.stem: Recidivism refers to:
options: the number of first-time offenders who are diverted from court
the process of releasing a young person from a youth detention centre
the time a young person spends on remand before their hearing
reoffending by a person who has already been dealt with for an offence
questions.explanation: High recidivism among young people who have been detained is a key argument for diversion and early intervention. Measures of success often compare reoffending rates between programs.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why detention is linked with higher recidivism for young people?
options: Detention is always too short to have any effect, so courts should impose much longer periods of custody
Detention centres are run by the young people themselves, so there is no supervision or support
Detention removes young people's criminal records, so they feel free to reoffend after release
Detention can disrupt education, family ties and work, and expose young people to more serious offenders
questions.explanation: Custody separates young people from the protective factors that help them desist, which is why international law treats detention as a last resort. Diversion aims to keep young people connected to school and family.

questions.stem: Which international instrument sets out the rights of children, including that detention should be a last resort?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights only
The Convention on the Rights of the Child
The International Covenant on Economic Rights
The Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination
questions.explanation: The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), ratified by Australia in 1990, says detention of a child should be a last resort and for the shortest appropriate time. It also protects the child's right to be heard and to have their best interests considered.

questions.stem: Under the Convention on the Rights of the Child, a child deprived of liberty should generally be:
options: held with adult prisoners so that they can learn from older people
kept in detention until their 18th birthday, whatever the offence
denied contact with their family so that their sentence is effective
separated from adults and treated with respect for their dignity
questions.explanation: Article 37 requires that children in custody be separated from adults unless that is not in their best interests and be able to keep contact with family. These standards inform NSW youth justice law.

questions.stem: Which Act sets out the main principles for dealing with children in criminal proceedings in NSW, including that a child's name must not be published?
options: Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998
Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987
Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999
Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002
questions.explanation: The Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) sets principles such as rehabilitation and the least restrictive response, and generally prohibits publishing the names of children involved in criminal proceedings. The care and protection Act deals with child welfare, not offending.

questions.stem: Which NSW statutory office promotes the rights and wellbeing of children and young people and advises government on issues affecting them?
options: The Advocate for Children and Young People
The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions
The NSW Commissioner of Police
The NSW Law Reform Commission
questions.explanation: The Advocate for Children and Young People, under the Advocate for Children and Young People Act 2014 (NSW), consults young people and advocates for their interests. The DPP prosecutes offences, and the Police Commissioner leads the police.

questions.stem: Which statement about the National Children's Commissioner is correct?
options: It is a UN body that sentences children who commit international crimes
It is a federal police unit that investigates offences committed by children
It is part of the Australian Human Rights Commission and promotes children's rights at a national level
It is a NSW court that hears criminal charges against children aged 10 to 17
questions.explanation: The National Children's Commissioner monitors children's rights in Australia and reports to the federal Parliament, including on youth justice. It advocates and reports but cannot make binding decisions.

questions.stem: When police question a child suspected of an offence in NSW, the child is generally entitled to:
options: be questioned by a magistrate instead of a police officer at the station
have a support person, such as a parent or other adult, present during questioning
refuse to give their name in all circumstances, because children are never required to
be released immediately without charge if they are under 16 years of age
questions.explanation: Children are vulnerable persons under LEPRA and its regulation, so a support person must generally be present for investigative procedures, and children can also contact a lawyer. These safeguards help ensure any admissions are reliable and voluntary.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the protections for young people during police questioning?
options: Support persons and legal advice help, but young people may not understand their rights or may feel pressured to talk
The protections remove all risk, because young people always understand cautions as well as adults do
The protections are unnecessary, because police in NSW are not permitted to question anyone under 18
The protections apply only to young people charged with murder, so most young people have none at all
questions.explanation: Young people may not fully understand a caution or may defer to authority, so safeguards are important but not complete. Legal services, such as Legal Aid's Youth Hotline, aim to give young people advice before they speak to police.

questions.stem: Which Act gives NSW police and courts the options of warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences for young offenders?
options: Children's Court Act 1987
Crimes Act 1900
Bail Act 2013
Young Offenders Act 1997
questions.explanation: The Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) sets up a hierarchy of diversionary options so that many young people are dealt with outside court. The aim is to address offending without the harmful effects of court and custody.

questions.stem: What happens in a youth justice conference under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)?
options: The young person meets the victim, family and police to discuss the harm and agree on an outcome plan
The young person is tried before a jury of other young people who decide whether they are guilty
The young person is sentenced to detention by a magistrate in a closed hearing of the Children's Court
The young person and police agree on a fine, which is paid without anyone else being present
questions.explanation: Conferences are a restorative justice process: the young person must admit the offence, and the plan may include an apology, reparation or a program. They aim to repair harm and reduce reoffending.

questions.stem: Which offence is excluded from the diversionary options of the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)?
options: An offence that results in the death of a person
Shoplifting a small item from a local supermarket
Malicious damage to a fence with graffiti
Possession of a small quantity of cannabis
questions.explanation: Serious offences such as those causing death and serious sexual offences are excluded, as are most traffic offences for young people old enough to hold a licence. Minor property offences and small-quantity cannabis possession can be dealt with under the Act.

questions.stem: The Children's Court of NSW mainly hears criminal matters involving young people who were:
options: aged under 25 at the time they were arrested
aged 18 to 21 at the time of the alleged offence
aged 10 to 17 at the time of the alleged offence
aged 5 to 21 at the time of the court hearing
questions.explanation: The Children's Court deals with offences committed by children aged 10 to 17, generally where they are charged before turning 21. Serious children's indictable offences, such as murder, are dealt with in higher courts.

questions.stem: Why are Children's Court criminal proceedings generally closed to the public?
options: To allow the magistrate to sentence the young person more harshly
To stop victims from finding out the outcome of the proceedings
To protect the young person's privacy and support rehabilitation
To prevent the young person's lawyer from hearing the evidence
questions.explanation: Closed hearings and the ban on publishing names protect young people from lasting stigma that could harm their chances of rehabilitation. Victims and others directly involved can still attend in many cases.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how sentencing in the Children's Court differs from adult sentencing?
options: Rehabilitation is given greater weight, and detention is used only as a last resort
Deterrence is the only purpose, so detention is the usual penalty for every offence
Young offenders cannot be given any penalty, so all charges are dismissed
Young offenders must serve the same maximum penalties as adults in adult prisons
questions.explanation: The Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) emphasises rehabilitation, education and the least restrictive response. Courts can still order detention in a youth detention centre for serious offending.

questions.stem: Justice reinvestment, such as the Maranguka project in Bourke, is best described as:
options: increasing police patrols and penalties to deter young people from offending
charging young offenders a fee to pay for their own supervision in the community
shifting resources from prisons to community programs that address the causes of offending
building more youth detention centres to remove young offenders from the wider community
questions.explanation: Justice reinvestment invests in local, community-led programs such as early intervention, education and support, aiming to reduce crime and incarceration. Maranguka is a community-led project in Bourke supported by Just Reinvest NSW.

questions.stem: What is the Youth Koori Court in the NSW Children's Court?
options: A separate court that hears trials of Aboriginal young people before a jury of community members only
A program that sends all Aboriginal young offenders to detention centres located on their own Country
A court that hears civil claims by Aboriginal young people against government departments
A process for eligible young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in which Elders help shape a plan before sentence
questions.explanation: The Youth Koori Court, first established at Parramatta in 2015, involves Elders and community members working with the young person on an action and support plan, and progress is considered at sentencing. It aims to address underlying issues and reduce reoffending.

questions.stem: Youth on Track is a NSW program that:
options: trains young people to work as police officers so that they can patrol their own communities
provides early intervention case management for young people at risk of becoming entrenched in offending
places all young people who have committed any offence in a youth detention centre for six months
allows young people to choose their own sentence from a list of options set by the magistrate
questions.explanation: Youth on Track works with young people aged 10 to 17 and their families to address risk factors such as disengagement from school and family issues. It reflects the view that early intervention is more effective than later punishment.

questions.stem: Which organisation provides free legal information and advice to young people in Australia?
options: The NSW Bar Association
The Judicial Commission of NSW
Youth Law Australia
The Law Council of Australia
questions.explanation: Youth Law Australia is a community legal service that gives young people free, confidential information and advice online and by phone. The Law Council and Bar Association are professional bodies for lawyers.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of NGOs such as the Shopfront Youth Legal Centre?
options: They make binding decisions in disputes involving young people, which replace the Children's Court
They prosecute young people on behalf of police, which ensures consistency in charging decisions
They are funded only by young people's fees, so they serve wealthy families before others
They provide free legal help and advocacy for disadvantaged young people, but demand exceeds their resources
questions.explanation: Youth legal NGOs represent young people who might otherwise be unrepresented and push for law reform, but limited funding means they cannot help everyone. They have no power to decide cases.

questions.stem: Which would be the best indicator that the youth justice system is achieving justice?
options: An increase in the number of young people charged with minor offences by police
Longer average periods of detention imposed on young people by the Children's Court
A fall in reoffending by young people diverted from court, without a rise in harm to the community
A rise in the number of young people held on remand in detention centres each year
questions.explanation: Success is measured by outcomes such as lower recidivism, protection of rights, community safety and efficient use of resources. More remand, more charges or longer detention would suggest the opposite.

questions.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people are heavily over-represented in NSW youth detention. Which statement best explains why this is a barrier to achieving justice?
options: It shows that the law applies different offences to Aboriginal young people than to others
It shows that Aboriginal young people are excluded from all diversionary programs by law
It shows that the Children's Court is not allowed to sentence non-Aboriginal young people
It suggests the system is not achieving equality, reflecting disadvantage and the effects of past policies
questions.explanation: The same laws apply to everyone, but over-representation points to unequal outcomes linked to social disadvantage, intergenerational trauma and differences in police contact and diversion. It is a long-standing concern noted by the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant barrier to young people achieving justice?
options: Young people can only make complaints about police through their school principal
Young people are not allowed to give evidence in any court, even as victims of crime
Lack of knowledge of their rights, limited resources and distrust of police and the legal system
Young people are prevented by law from contacting any lawyer at all until they turn 18 years old
questions.explanation: Young people often do not know their rights, cannot afford lawyers and may distrust authorities, which limits their ability to use the system. Free youth legal services and hotlines aim to reduce these barriers.

questions.stem: A teenage worker is underpaid but does not complain because she fears losing her job and does not know where to get help. Which barrier to justice does this best show?
options: The limit on the number of cautions under the Young Offenders Act
Lack of awareness and a power imbalance between young people and adults
The age of criminal responsibility being set too low under current NSW law
The closed nature of hearings in the Children's Court of NSW
questions.explanation: Young people often have less knowledge, confidence and bargaining power than adults, which discourages them from enforcing their rights. Services such as Youth Law Australia and the Fair Work Ombudsman can help.
